title: Italian grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday fluency, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is the Italian spoken in Italy today, with its accents written as they should be.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Italian conversation.
lessons.topic: {{sono, sei, è}} (“I am, you are, he/she is”), with no word for “I”; {{mi chiamo}}; {{di}} + a city

goal.t: Ciao, sono Anna. Sono di Londra.
goal.tr: Hi, I'm Anna. I'm from London.

dialog.tr: Hi! I'm Marco.
Hi, Marco. I'm Anna.
Where are you from?
I'm from London. And you?
I'm from Rome. Nice to meet you!
Nice to meet you too!

blocks.p: **I am, you are.** {{sono}} means “I am” and {{sei}} “you are” (to a friend). Notice that Anna often doesn't say a word for “I”: {{sono di Londra}} is, word for word, “am from London”. The verb itself already says who.

blocks.means: a word for doing or being: am, live, eat, go.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she.

table: {{io}} “I” only to stress it: {{Io sono di Roma}} “I'm from Rome (and you aren't)”
to a friend, a child, a relative

blocks.p: **Your name.** {{Sono Anna}} or {{Mi chiamo Anna}}, word for word “I call myself Anna”. To ask a friend: {{Come ti chiami?}} “What's your name?”

**Where you're from.** {{di}} + a city: {{Sono di Roma}}. For a country, say your nationality: {{Sono inglese}}, {{Sono americano}} (said by a man), {{Sono americana}} (said by a woman). Italian writes nationalities with a small letter.

ex.note: a question just by raising your voice at the end

ex.t: Lui è Paolo. È di Napoli.
ex.tr: This is Paolo. He's from Naples.

blocks.tip: The accent matters: {{è}} “is” and {{e}} “and” are two different words. Italian accents are part of the spelling, like the dot on an i.

mistakes.why: With {{sono}}, “from” is {{di}}. ({{da}} goes with {{vengo}} “I come”: {{Vengo da Londra}}.)
“Is” is {{è}}, with its accent; {{e}} without it means “and”.

practice.q: You want to say “I'm from Rome”. Which one?
practice.why: {{sono}} is “I am”; {{sei}} is “you are” and {{è}} “he or she is”.

lessons.title: Greet people, casually or politely
lessons.summary: Say hello, ask how someone is and say goodbye, to a friend and to a stranger: the two Italian ways of saying “you”.
lessons.topic: {{tu}} (casual “you”) and {{Lei}} (polite “you”); {{stare}} in {{come stai? / come sta?}}

goal.t: Buongiorno, signora Rossi! Come sta?
goal.tr: Good morning, Mrs. Rossi! How are you?

dialog.tr: Hi, Sara! How are you?
Fine, thanks. And you?
Not bad.
Good morning, Mr. Bianchi. How are you?
Very well, thank you. And you?
Fine, thank you.

blocks.p: **Two ways to say “you”.** Italian has a casual “you”, {{tu}}, for friends, family, children and people your age in relaxed places, and a polite one, {{Lei}}, for strangers, older people, shop and hotel staff, and anyone you'd call Mr. or Mrs. {{Lei}} takes the same verb as “she”: {{Come sta?}} is, word for word, “How is she?”, and it means “How are you?” said politely.
**“How are you” uses {{stare}}**, not {{essere}}: {{stai}} for {{tu}}, {{sta}} for {{Lei}}, and the answer {{sto bene}} “I'm fine”, or simply {{bene}}.

blocks.tip: When in doubt, start with {{Lei}}. If the other person prefers {{tu}}, they'll say so: {{Diamoci del tu!}} “Let's use tu!”. Young people use {{tu}} with each other straight away. {{Lei}} is often written with a capital L, to tell it apart from {{lei}} “she”.

mistakes.tr: Good morning, madam. How are you?
mistakes.why: To a stranger or an older person, use the polite {{sta}} ({{Lei}}), not {{stai}}.
“I'm fine” uses {{stare}}: {{sto bene}}. {{Sono bene}} isn't Italian.

practice.q: You meet your friend's grandmother for the first time. You say…
practice.why: A stranger and an older person: {{buongiorno}}, and the polite {{sta}}.

lessons.title: Order at the café
lessons.summary: Ask for a coffee, a pastry or a drink, politely: “I'd like a cappuccino, please.”
lessons.topic: {{vorrei}} “I'd like”; masculine and feminine nouns; “a”: {{un, uno, una, un'}}

goal.t: Vorrei un cappuccino e una spremuta, per favore.
goal.tr: I'd like a cappuccino and a fresh orange juice, please.

dialog.tr: Good morning! What will you have?

dialog.t: Vorrei un cappuccino e un cornetto, per favore.
dialog.tr: I'd like a cappuccino and a croissant, please.
Anything else?
Yes, a small bottle of water.
Here you are.
Thanks!

blocks.p: **{{Vorrei}}** is the polite “I'd like”: the word to use in a café, a shop or a hotel. Put what you want after it: {{vorrei un caffè}}. Add {{per favore}} “please”.

blocks.means: a word for a person, a thing, an animal or a place: coffee, girl, dog, Rome.
in Italian every noun is either masculine or feminine, even the names of things. It's a fact about the word, not the thing: {{tavolo}} “table” is masculine, {{sedia}} “chair” is feminine.

blocks.p: **Masculine or feminine?** The ending usually tells you: most nouns ending in {{-o}} are masculine ({{cornetto}}, {{panino}}), most ending in {{-a}} are feminine ({{pizza}}, {{birra}}). Nouns ending in {{-e}} can be either ({{latte}} “milk” is masculine, {{notte}} “night” feminine), and a few are simply worth learning ({{caffè}} and {{tè}} are masculine).
**“A” changes with the noun.** Italian has four forms of “a”, chosen by the noun's gender and its first sound:

table: masculine nouns starting with s + consonant, or z
feminine nouns starting with a vowel

ex.tr: I'd like a sandwich and a water.

blocks.tip: In Italy, {{un caffè}} is an espresso. Want a little milk in it? Ask for {{un caffè macchiato}}. And be careful: {{un latte}} is just a glass of milk!

mistakes.why: {{caffè}} is masculine, even though it doesn't end in -o: {{un}}.
{{acqua}} is feminine: {{una}}, which becomes {{un'}} (with an apostrophe) before a vowel. A masculine noun has no apostrophe: {{un amico}}.
{{voglio}} “I want” is correct Italian, but it sounds blunt when you order. {{vorrei}} is the polite way.

practice.tr: I'd like a fresh orange juice, please.
A spritz for me.
practice.why: A masculine noun starting with s + consonant: {{uno}}.

lessons.title: Say where you live and what you do
lessons.summary: Tell someone where you live, what languages you speak and where you work or study: your first verbs.
lessons.topic: The present of -are verbs ({{parlo, parli, parla…}}); the ending says who

goal.t: Abito a Londra e lavoro in banca.
goal.tr: I live in London and I work in a bank.

dialog.tr: Where do you live?

dialog.t: Adesso abito a Bologna. E tu?
dialog.tr: I live in Bologna now. And you?
Me too. Do you work here?

dialog.t: Sì, lavoro in un ristorante. E studio italiano!
dialog.tr: Yes, I work in a restaurant. And I'm studying Italian!
You speak very well!

blocks.means: the basic form of a verb, the one in the dictionary: to live, to work. In Italian it ends in -are, -ere or -ire: {{parlare}} “to speak”, {{prendere}} “to take”, {{dormire}} “to sleep”.

blocks.p: **The ending says who.** To use a verb, take off {{-are}} and add the ending for the person. Most verbs ending in {{-are}} work exactly like these two:

blocks.means: who or what does the action of the verb: in “Anna works”, Anna is the subject.

blocks.p: Because the ending says who the subject is, Italians usually leave out {{io}} “I”, {{tu}} “you” and the rest: {{Parlo inglese}} “I speak English”. Say them only to stress or to contrast: {{Io lavoro, e tu?}} “I work, and you?”

**One present for two.** {{lavoro}} is both “I work” and “I'm working”, {{studio italiano}} both “I study Italian” and “I'm studying Italian”. And a question needs no “do”: {{Lavori qui?}} “Do you work here?”

ex.t: Parlo inglese e un po' di italiano.
ex.tr: I speak English and a little Italian.

blocks.tip: Living in a city: {{a}}; in a country: {{in}}. {{Abito a Milano, in Italia}} “I live in Milan, in Italy”.

mistakes.why: Use the verb with its ending ({{abito}}), not the dictionary form; and {{io}} isn't needed.
For he or she, the ending is {{-a}}: {{lavora}}. {{lavoro}} means “I work”.

practice.tr: Anna works in an office.

lessons.title: Get to know someone
lessons.summary: Ask where someone is from, where they live, what they do and why they're here, to a friend or politely.
lessons.topic: Questions: the voice going up, and the question words {{chi, cosa, dove, quando, come, perché, quanto}}

goal.t: Di dove sei? E che lavoro fai?
goal.tr: Where are you from? And what do you do for a living?

dialog.tr: What's your name?
My name's Sam. And you?
Elena. Where are you from?
I'm from Dublin.
And why are you in Italy?

dialog.t: Studio italiano a Siena. Tu che lavoro fai?
dialog.tr: I'm studying Italian in Siena. What do you do?
I'm a teacher.

blocks.p: **Yes-or-no questions** look exactly like statements: only your voice changes, going up at the end. {{Parli inglese.}} “You speak English.” {{Parli inglese?}} “Do you speak English?” There is no word for “do”.
**Question words** come first:

table: {{Perché studi italiano?}} “Why are you studying Italian?”

blocks.p: {{perché}} means both “why?” and “because”: {{Perché studi italiano? Perché amo l'Italia!}} “Why are you studying Italian? Because I love Italy!”

**To someone you call {{Lei}}**, the verb takes the “he, she” ending: {{Di dov'è?}} “Where are you from?”, {{Dove abita?}} “Where do you live?”, {{Che lavoro fa?}} “What do you do?” ({{fai}} and {{fa}} come from {{fare}} “to do, to make”, a verb you'll meet again.)

ex.note: polite: {{è}} for “you are”; {{dov'è}} is {{dove è}} run together
polite; to a friend, {{Come ti chiami?}}

ex.tr: What do you do? I'm a doctor.
ex.note: after {{sono}}, a job usually has no “a”

blocks.tip: A question that needs “from” starts with it: {{Di dove sei?}} is, word for word, “Of where are you?”. Italian never leaves a little word like {{di}} at the end of a question.

mistakes.why: The little word {{di}} goes at the start of the question, with {{dove}}.
{{perché}} needs its accent: é, sloping up to the right.

lessons.title: Ask where things are
lessons.summary: Find the station, the bathroom or your hotel: “Excuse me, where's the station?”
lessons.topic: “The”: {{il, lo, la, l'}}; {{dov'è…?}}

goal.t: Scusi, dov'è la stazione?
goal.tr: Excuse me, where's the station?

dialog.tr: Excuse me, where's the bathroom?
It's over there, on the right.
And the exit?
The exit is on the left.
Thanks a lot!
You're welcome!

blocks.p: **{{Dov'è…?}}** “Where is…?” is {{dove}} + {{è}} run together. Then the thing you're looking for, with “the”.

blocks.means: a little word before a noun: “a, an” and “the”. Italian articles change with the noun's gender and its first sound.

blocks.p: **“The” has four forms in the singular**, chosen like the forms of “a”:

table: masculine nouns starting with s + consonant, or z
any noun starting with a vowel

blocks.p: So the pairs go together: {{un treno, il treno}}; {{uno stadio, lo stadio}}; {{una banca, la banca}}; {{un albergo, l'albergo}} and {{un'uscita, l'uscita}}. Nouns ending in {{-ione}} are feminine: {{la stazione}}, {{la lezione}}.

ex.t: La stazione è lì, a destra.
ex.tr: The station is over there, on the right.

blocks.tip: {{Scusi}} “excuse me” is for someone you call {{Lei}}; to a friend, {{scusa}}. The answers you'll hear: {{qui}} “here”, {{lì}} “there”, {{a destra}} “on the right”, {{a sinistra}} “on the left”, {{dritto}} “straight ahead”, {{vicino}} “near”, {{lontano}} “far”.

mistakes.why: {{stazione}} is feminine (like most nouns in {{-ione}}): {{la}}.
Before a vowel, “the” is {{l'}}: {{l'albergo}}.
A masculine noun starting with z: {{lo}}.

lessons.title: Describe things and people
lessons.summary: Say what something or someone is like: big, small, nice, expensive, open, tired.
lessons.topic: Adjectives agree with the noun ({{piccolo, piccola}}); where they go; {{molto}}

goal.t: Il ristorante è piccolo, ma la pizza è buona!
goal.tr: The restaurant is small, but the pizza is good!

dialog.tr: What's the new apartment like?

dialog.t: È piccolo, ma è molto bello.
dialog.tr: It's small, but it's very nice.
And the neighborhood?

dialog.t: La zona è tranquilla e non è cara.
dialog.tr: The neighborhood is quiet, and it isn't expensive.
Lucky you!

blocks.means: a word that describes a noun: big, red, nice, Italian.
one word changing its ending to match another. In Italian, adjectives agree with their noun: masculine with masculine, feminine with feminine.

blocks.p: **Describing words agree.** Adjectives ending in {{-o}} change to {{-a}} for a feminine noun: {{il ristorante è piccolo}}, {{la cucina è piccola}}. Adjectives ending in {{-e}} stay the same for both: {{il libro è interessante}}, {{la città è interessante}}.

**After the noun.** Most adjectives come after the noun: {{un vino rosso}} “a red wine”, {{una ragazza simpatica}} “a nice girl”. A few very common ones often go before it: {{bello}}, {{grande}}, {{piccolo}}, {{nuovo}}, {{vecchio}}, {{buono}}: {{una bella città}} “a beautiful city”, {{un buon caffè}} “a good coffee” ({{buono}} shortens to {{buon}} before a masculine noun, just as {{uno}} shortens to {{un}}).
**{{molto}}** “very” goes before the adjective: {{molto bello}}. And {{non}} goes before {{è}}: {{non è caro}} “it isn't expensive”.

ex.note: {{intelligente}} ends in -e: the same for a man or a woman
said by a woman; a man says {{sono stanco}}

blocks.tip: Adjectives about you agree with you: a man says {{sono stanco}}, {{sono contento}} “I'm happy”; a woman says {{sono stanca}}, {{sono contenta}}.

mistakes.why: {{pizza}} is feminine, so the adjective ends in {{-a}}.
Colors, like most adjectives, come after the noun.

lessons.title: Talk about more than one
lessons.summary: Order for the whole table, buy two tickets, and say what “we” and “they” are like.
lessons.topic: Plurals ({{-i, -e}}); “the”: {{i, gli, le}}; {{siamo, siete, sono}}

goal.t: Vorrei due biglietti per Firenze, per favore.
goal.tr: I'd like two tickets to Florence, please.

dialog.tr: Good evening! How many of you are there?
There are three of us.

dialog.t: Prego, i tavoli fuori sono liberi.
dialog.tr: Please, the tables outside are free.

dialog.t: Perfetto! Vorremmo tre menù, per favore.
dialog.tr: Perfect! We'd like three menus, please.

dialog.t: Ecco i menù. Le pizze sono molto buone!
dialog.tr: Here are the menus. The pizzas are very good!

blocks.p: **Plurals change the last vowel**, never add -s: {{-o}} becomes {{-i}}, {{-a}} becomes {{-e}}, {{-e}} becomes {{-i}}.

table: no change: an accent at the end, or a foreign word

blocks.p: **“The” in the plural.** {{il}} becomes {{i}}; masculine {{lo}} and {{l'}} become {{gli}}; {{la}} and feminine {{l'}} become {{le}}: {{lo studente, gli studenti}}; {{l'aereo, gli aerei}}; {{l'uscita, le uscite}}. Adjectives go into the plural with their noun: {{i tavoli liberi}}, {{le birre fredde}}.
**We, you, they.** Here is all of {{essere}}. Yes, {{sono}} is both “I am” and “they are”: the rest of the sentence makes it clear.

ex.t: I negozi sono chiusi la domenica.
ex.tr: The stores are closed on Sundays.

ex.t: Due cappuccini e due cornetti, per favore.
ex.tr: Two cappuccinos and two croissants, please.

blocks.tip: A group of men and women takes the masculine plural: {{Marco e Giulia sono italiani}}. The feminine plural is only for a group of women, or of feminine things.

mistakes.why: The noun changes too: {{pizza}}, {{pizze}}.
Before s + consonant, z or a vowel, the masculine plural “the” is {{gli}}.
Italian never adds -s, and nouns ending in an accented vowel don't change at all.

lessons.title: Say what you have, your age, and how you feel
lessons.summary: Check in with your reservation, say how old you are, and say you're hungry, thirsty or cold: in Italian, you “have” them.
lessons.topic: {{avere}} “to have”; {{ho trent'anni}}, {{ho fame}}, {{ho freddo}} (and {{fa freddo}})

goal.t: Ho venticinque anni e ho una sorella.
goal.tr: I'm twenty-five and I have a sister.

dialog.tr: Good evening. Do you have a reservation?

dialog.t: Sì, ho una prenotazione a nome Smith.
dialog.tr: Yes, I have a reservation under the name Smith.
Perfect. Do you have any suitcases?

dialog.t: Sì, due. E abbiamo fame: il ristorante è aperto?
dialog.tr: Yes, two. And we're hungry: is the restaurant open?
Yes, until ten.

blocks.means: a verb whose forms don't follow the usual pattern, so you learn them one by one.

blocks.p: **{{avere}} “to have”** is irregular: learn its forms by heart. Its {{h}} is never pronounced; it's there only to tell {{ho}} “I have” from {{o}} “or”, {{hai}} from {{ai}} “to the”, and {{ha}} from {{a}} “to”.
**Where English says “I am”, Italian often says “I have”.** Your age is something you have: {{Ho trent'anni}} “I'm thirty”, word for word “I have thirty years”. So are hunger, thirst, heat and cold:
To ask someone's age: {{Quanti anni hai?}} “How old are you?”, word for word “How many years do you have?”

ex.t: Ho una sorella e un fratello.
ex.tr: I have a sister and a brother.
Do you have a room for tonight?

blocks.tip: The weather is different: {{Fa freddo}} “It's cold (out)” uses {{fare}}. {{Ho freddo}} is how you feel; {{fa freddo}} is the weather.

mistakes.why: Age uses {{avere}}: “I have thirty years”.
Hunger is something you have: {{ho fame}}.
“I have” is written {{ho}}, with a silent h; {{o}} means “or”.

practice.tr: How old are you?

practice.why: How you feel: {{ho freddo}}. {{Fa freddo}} is “it's cold”, the weather.

lessons.title: Say what there is
lessons.summary: Ask if there's an ATM, a pharmacy or a free table nearby, and understand the answer: “there is”, “there are”.
lessons.topic: {{c'è}} “there is”, {{ci sono}} “there are”; {{non c'è}}; {{c'è}} or {{è}}

goal.t: C'è un bancomat qui vicino?
goal.tr: Is there an ATM near here?

dialog.t: Scusi, c'è una farmacia qui vicino?

blocks.p: **{{c'è}} “there is”** ({{ci}} + {{è}}) for one thing, **{{ci sono}} “there are”** for more than one. Put {{non}} first for “there isn't, there aren't”.

table: {{Ci sono due bagni.}} “There are two bathrooms.”

blocks.p: **{{c'è}} or {{è}}?** {{c'è}} says that something exists or is somewhere; {{è}} says what or how something is. {{C'è un museo}} “There's a museum”; {{È un museo}} “It's a museum”.
On the phone, {{c'è}} asks if someone is there: {{C'è Marco?}} “Is Marco there?” {{No, non c'è.}} “No, he isn't (here).”

ex.t: Ci sono molti turisti in agosto.
ex.tr: There are a lot of tourists in August.
Is there Wi-Fi in the room?

blocks.tip: No word for “any” is needed: {{Ci sono negozi?}} “Are there any stores?”; {{Non c'è pane}} “There isn't any bread”.

lessons.title: Ask the price and pay
lessons.summary: Ask how much things cost, understand the numbers, and pay: “How much are the tickets?”
lessons.topic: Numbers; {{quanto costa?}} / {{quanto costano?}}; {{quanti, quante}}

goal.t: Scusi, quanto costano i biglietti?
goal.tr: Excuse me, how much are the tickets?

dialog.tr: Good morning. How much is the newspaper?
Two euros.
And the postcards?

dialog.t: Le cartoline costano un euro e cinquanta.

dialog.t: Allora, il giornale e tre cartoline. Quant'è?

blocks.p: **How much?** {{Quanto costa?}} for one thing, {{Quanto costano?}} for more than one: the verb {{costare}} “to cost” agrees with what you're buying. When you pay for everything together: {{Quant'è?}} “How much is it?”

**The tens**: {{trenta}} 30, {{quaranta}} 40, {{cinquanta}} 50, {{sessanta}} 60, {{settanta}} 70, {{ottanta}} 80, {{novanta}} 90, {{cento}} 100, {{mille}} 1,000. In between, just join them: {{ventidue}} 22, {{trentacinque}} 35. Two small rules: a ten drops its last vowel before {{uno}} and {{otto}} ({{ventuno}}, {{ventotto}}), and a {{tre}} at the end takes an accent ({{ventitré}}, {{trentatré}}).
**Prices**: {{euro}} never changes: {{un euro}}, {{dieci euro}}. Cents are {{centesimi}}, but people usually just say the numbers: {{tre euro e cinquanta}} “three fifty”.
**How many?** {{quanto}} agrees with its noun, like an adjective: {{Quanti biglietti?}} “How many tickets?”, {{Quante persone?}} “How many people?”

blocks.tip: Prices are written with a comma: {{2,50 €}} is two euros fifty, said {{due e cinquanta}}.

{{euro}} doesn't change in the plural.

lessons.title: Say where you're going
lessons.summary: Tell someone where you're going (to Rome, to Italy, to the beach, to the doctor's) and suggest going somewhere together.
lessons.topic: {{andare}} “to go”; {{a}} Roma, {{in}} Italia, {{al}} mare, {{dal}} medico

goal.t: Stasera vado al cinema con Marco.
goal.tr: Tonight I'm going to the movies with Marco.

dialog.tr: Hi! Where are you going?

blocks.p: **{{andare}} “to go”** is irregular, and you'll use it every day:

blocks.means: a little word that shows place, direction or time: to, in, on, from, with.

blocks.p: **To where?** Italian chooses the preposition by the kind of place:

table: {{in centro, in banca, in farmacia, in ufficio, in vacanza}}
{{al cinema, al mare, alla stazione, all'aeroporto}}

blocks.p: **{{a}} and “the” become one word**: {{a + il = al}}, {{a + la = alla}}, {{a + l' = all'}}. The same happens with {{da}}: {{da + il = dal}}. The next lesson shows the whole pattern.
**{{andiamo}}** also means “let's go”: {{Andiamo!}} And {{Andiamo al mare?}} suggests it: “Shall we go to the beach?”

ex.tr: I'm going to Milan by train.
ex.note: by train, by car: {{in treno, in macchina}}

blocks.tip: As in English, the present works for plans: {{Domani vado a Firenze}} “Tomorrow I'm going to Florence”.

mistakes.why: Countries take {{in}}; cities take {{a}}.
Home is just {{a casa}}, with no “the”.
{{andare}} is irregular: “I go” is {{vado}}.

lessons.title: Say exactly where things are
lessons.summary: On the table, in the bag, in front of the church, next to the phone: find things and tell others where they are.
lessons.topic: Prepositions joined to “the”: {{nel, sul, al, dal, del}}…; {{vicino a, davanti a, sotto}}

goal.t: Le chiavi sono sul tavolo, vicino al telefono.
goal.tr: The keys are on the table, next to the phone.

dialog.tr: Where are the keys?
They're on the table, in the kitchen.
No, they aren't there.

dialog.t: Allora sono nella borsa, o nel cassetto.

dialog.t: Ah, ecco! Sono nella tasca della giacca.

blocks.p: **The prepositions for place** are {{in}} “in”, {{su}} “on”, {{a}} “at, to”, {{da}} “from, at someone's”, and {{di}} “of”. Before “the”, they join it to make one word:

It looks like a lot, but the pattern is simple: the preposition + the article, with {{in}} turning into {{ne-}} and {{di}} into {{de-}}, and a double l whenever the article starts with l ({{la}} → {{nella}}).

**No “the”, nothing to join**: city names ({{a Roma}}) and many everyday places ({{in cucina}}, {{in centro}}, {{a casa}}). With “the”, for one particular thing, they join: {{nella cucina di Marco}} “in Marco's kitchen”.

**Where exactly**: {{vicino a}} “near, next to”, {{davanti a}} “in front of”, {{in fondo a}} “at the end of”, {{dietro}} “behind”, {{sotto}} “under”, {{sopra}} “on top of”, {{tra}} “between”. The ones with {{a}} join it to “the”: {{vicino al telefono}}, {{davanti alla stazione}}.

ex.t: Il gatto è sotto il letto.
ex.tr: The cat is under the bed.

ex.t: Il bagno è in fondo al corridoio.
ex.tr: The bathroom is at the end of the hallway.
I live in the old town.

ex.t: La farmacia è davanti alla chiesa.
ex.tr: The pharmacy is in front of the church.
The menu is on the table.
See you in front of the movie theater.

blocks.tip: {{di}} + “the” can also mean “some”: {{Vorrei del pane}} “I'd like some bread”. You'll hear it in stores.

mistakes.tr: The keys are on the table.

lessons.title: Tell the time and make an appointment
lessons.summary: Ask and say the time, say when things open and start, and book a table or an appointment.
lessons.topic: {{Che ore sono? Sono le tre, è l'una}}; {{alle otto}}; the days of the week

goal.t: Il treno parte alle otto e mezza.
goal.tr: The train leaves at eight thirty.

dialog.tr: Doctor's office, good morning.

dialog.t: Buongiorno. Vorrei un appuntamento con la dottoressa Neri.
dialog.tr: Good morning. I'd like an appointment with Dr. Neri.
Is Thursday at three OK?

dialog.t: Alle tre no, lavoro. Alle cinque?
dialog.tr: Not at three, I'm working. At five?
All right: Thursday at five.
Perfect, thanks a lot!

blocks.p: **What time is it?** {{Che ore sono?}} (or {{Che ora è?}}). The answer is {{sono le}} + the hour, because hours are counted as feminine plural: {{sono le tre}} “it's three o'clock”. Only one o'clock is singular: {{è l'una}}. And {{è mezzogiorno}} “it's noon”, {{è mezzanotte}} “it's midnight”.

**At what time?** {{A che ora…?}}, and the answer with {{alle}} ({{a + le}}): {{alle otto}} “at eight”, {{all'una}} “at one”, {{a mezzogiorno}} “at noon”. Timetables and stores use the 24-hour clock: {{alle diciotto}} “at 6 p.m.”.
**The days**: {{lunedì, martedì, mercoledì, giovedì, venerdì, sabato, domenica}}, with no capital letter. {{Lunedì}} alone means “on Monday”, this one; {{il lunedì}} means “on Mondays”, every week.

ex.t: Che ore sono? Sono le dieci.
ex.tr: What time is it? It's ten o'clock.

ex.t: A che ora apre il museo?
ex.tr: What time does the museum open?

ex.t: Apre alle nove e chiude alle diciannove.
ex.tr: It opens at nine and closes at 7 p.m.
See you on Saturday at eight.

ex.t: Il lunedì il ristorante è chiuso.
ex.tr: The restaurant is closed on Mondays.

blocks.tip: “Ten-ish” is {{verso le dieci}} “around ten”. {{In orario}} means “on time”, {{in ritardo}} “late”.

mistakes.why: Hours are plural: {{sono le tre}}. Only one o'clock is singular: {{è l'una}}.
One o'clock is {{l'una}}, and {{a + l'}} = {{all'}}.

lessons.title: Talk about your daily habits
lessons.summary: Say how you get to work, what you read, when you finish, and that you don't understand: verbs in -ere and -ire.
lessons.topic: The present of -ere and -ire verbs ({{prendo, dormo}}); {{capisco, finisco}} with -isc-

goal.t: La mattina prendo l'autobus e leggo il giornale.
goal.tr: In the morning I take the bus and read the paper.

dialog.tr: How do you get to work?
I take the subway. And you?

dialog.t: Io vado a piedi. Ma la sera prendo il tram, perché finisco tardi.
dialog.tr: I walk. But in the evening I take the tram, because I finish late.
What time do you finish?

dialog.t: Alle otto. E poi dormo sul divano!
dialog.tr: At eight. And then I fall asleep on the sofa!

blocks.p: **Verbs in -ere and -ire** have the same endings as -are verbs for “I” ({{-o}}), “you” ({{-i}}) and “we” ({{-iamo}}); the others change a little:

**Two kinds of -ire verbs.** Some, like {{dormire}}, {{partire}} “to leave” and {{aprire}} “to open”, take the endings directly. Others, like {{finire}}, {{capire}} “to understand” and {{preferire}} “to prefer”, add {{-isc-}} in four of their forms: {{capisco, capisci, capisce, capiscono}}. A dictionary tells you which; the common ones are few.
**Saying it**: {{sc}} sounds like “sk” before o and a, and like “sh” before i and e: {{capisco}} “ka-PEE-sko”, {{capisci}} “ka-PEE-shee”.

ex.tr: I read a book every evening.
Do you write a lot of emails?

ex.t: Luca dorme fino a tardi la domenica.

blocks.tip: {{Non capisco}} and {{Può ripetere, per favore?}} “Could you repeat that, please?” will save you in many conversations.

mistakes.why: {{capire}} adds {{-isc-}}: {{capisco}}.
-ere and -ire verbs end in {{-e}} for he and she ({{prende}}); {{-a}} is the ending of -are verbs ({{parla}}).

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.summary: Say what you like and don't like, ask others, and agree: “Me too!”, “Me neither!”
lessons.topic: {{mi piace}} / {{mi piacciono}} (back to front: “it pleases me”); {{ti piace? Le piace?}}; {{anche a me, neanche a me}}

goal.t: Mi piace molto il caffè, ma non mi piacciono i dolci.
goal.tr: I really like coffee, but I don't like sweets.

dialog.tr: Do you like Italian food?
Yes, I love it!

dialog.t: E ti piacciono i film italiani?
dialog.tr: And do you like Italian movies?

dialog.t: Sì, e mi piace anche leggere in italiano.

dialog.t: Anche a me! Non mi piace il calcio, però.
dialog.tr: Me too! I don't like soccer, though.

blocks.p: **Back to front.** {{mi piace}} works like “it pleases me”: the thing you like is the subject, and the verb agrees with it. For one thing, or for doing something: {{mi piace}}. For more than one thing: {{mi piacciono}}.

**“The” for things in general.** Italian uses “the” when you talk about something in general: {{Mi piace il caffè}} “I like coffee”, {{Mi piacciono i cani}} “I like dogs”. English leaves “the” out there; Italian keeps it. (Cities have no article: {{Mi piace Roma}}.)
**Liking to do something**: {{mi piace}} + the infinitive: {{Mi piace cucinare}} “I like cooking”.
**Agreeing and disagreeing**: {{Anche a me!}} “Me too!”; {{Neanche a me!}} “Me neither!” (to something you don't like); {{A me sì!}} “I do!”; {{A me no!}} “I don't!”

ex.t: A Marco piacciono le macchine sportive.

blocks.tip: For “I love” about food and places, Italians usually say {{mi piace tantissimo}} or {{adoro}}: {{Adoro la pizza!}} {{Amo}} is mostly for people.

mistakes.why: Start with {{mi}}: “coffee pleases me”.
{{i film}} is plural, so the verb is too: {{piacciono}}.
Talking about something in general, Italian keeps “the”.

lessons.summary: Talk about your habits: always, often, sometimes, never, nothing, nobody, not anymore.
lessons.topic: {{non}}; {{sempre, spesso, a volte, mai}}; the double negative {{non… mai, non… niente, non… nessuno, non… più}}

goal.t: Non bevo mai caffè la sera.

dialog.tr: Do you smoke?

blocks.p: **{{non}}** goes right before the verb: {{Non fumo}} “I don't smoke”. That's all Italian needs for “don't” and “doesn't”.

**How often**: {{sempre}} “always”, {{spesso}} “often”, {{a volte}} or {{qualche volta}} “sometimes”, {{raramente}} “rarely”, {{mai}} “never”. They usually go after the verb: {{Vado spesso al cinema}} “I often go to the movies”.

**Two negatives, one meaning.** With {{mai}} “never”, {{niente}} “nothing”, {{nessuno}} “nobody” and {{più}} “anymore”, Italian keeps {{non}} before the verb as well: {{Non bevo mai caffè}}, word for word “I don't drink never coffee”. This double negative is correct, standard Italian.

table: I don't live in Rome anymore.

ex.tr: I often go to the beach.

blocks.tip: {{bere}} “to drink” uses an old stem, {{bev-}}: {{bevo, bevi, beve, beviamo, bevete, bevono}}.

mistakes.why: With {{mai}}, keep {{non}} before the verb too.
{{non}} before the verb, {{mai}} after it.

lessons.title: Make plans and invite someone
lessons.summary: Ask what someone is doing this weekend, invite them, and say yes or no nicely.
lessons.topic: {{fare, uscire, venire}}; the present for plans; {{ti va di…?}}; the weather with {{fa}}

goal.t: Stasera esco con gli amici. Vieni anche tu?
goal.tr: I'm going out with friends tonight. Are you coming too?

dialog.tr: What are you doing on Saturday?
Nothing special. Why?

dialog.t: Facciamo una festa a casa mia. Vieni?
dialog.tr: We're having a party at my place. Are you coming?

dialog.t: Sì, vengo volentieri! A che ora?
dialog.tr: Yes, I'd love to come! What time?

dialog.t: Alle nove. Se fa bel tempo, stiamo in terrazza.
dialog.tr: At nine. If the weather's nice, we'll be out on the terrace.
Perfect, see you Saturday!

blocks.p: **Three irregular verbs for plans**: {{fare}} “to do, to make”, {{uscire}} “to go out”, {{venire}} “to come”.

**The present for plans.** Italian uses the ordinary present for arranged plans, where English says “I'm going out tonight”: {{Stasera esco}}, {{Domani faccio la spesa}} “Tomorrow I'm doing the grocery shopping”.

**Inviting**: {{Vieni…?}} “Are you coming…?”, {{Usciamo stasera?}} “Shall we go out tonight?”, and {{Ti va di…?}} “Do you feel like…?” + the infinitive: {{Ti va di andare al cinema?}}. The answers: {{Sì, volentieri!}} “I'd love to!”, {{Mi dispiace, non posso}} “Sorry, I can't”.

**{{fare}} is everywhere**: {{fare colazione}} “to have breakfast”, {{fare la doccia}} “to take a shower”, {{fare una passeggiata}} “to go for a walk”, {{fare la spesa}} “to do the grocery shopping”. And the weather: {{Che tempo fa?}} “What's the weather like?”, {{Fa bel tempo}} “It's nice out”, {{Fa caldo}} “It's hot”.

lessons.title: Talk about your family
lessons.summary: Show photos and say who's who: my sister, our parents, their house. Possessives, and when they lose “the”.
lessons.topic: Possessives: {{il mio, la mia, i miei, le mie}}…; {{mia madre}} without the article

goal.t: Mia sorella si chiama Laura e i miei genitori abitano a Boston.
goal.tr: My sister's name is Laura, and my parents live in Boston.

dialog.tr: Who's she?

dialog.t: È mia sorella, Laura. E loro sono i suoi figli.
dialog.tr: That's my sister, Laura. And they're her children.

dialog.t: Che carini! E lui è tuo padre?
dialog.tr: How cute! And is he your father?

dialog.t: Sì, e lei è mia madre. La loro casa è al mare.
dialog.tr: Yes, and she's my mother. Their house is by the sea.
What a lovely family!

blocks.means: a word that says whose something is: my, your, his, our.

blocks.p: **My, your, his…** In Italian, the possessive usually comes with “the”: {{il mio libro}} “my book”, word for word “the my book”. And it agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner:
**His or her?** {{suo}} means both, and agrees with the thing: {{la sua macchina}} is “his car” or “her car”, because {{macchina}} is feminine. The conversation tells you whose.

**Family: no “the”.** With one member of the family, leave out the article: {{mia madre}}, {{mio padre}}, {{mio fratello}}, {{tua sorella}}. Keep it in the plural ({{i miei genitori}}), with {{loro}} ({{il loro figlio}}), and with pet names ({{la mia mamma}}, {{il mio papà}}).

ex.tr: His car is new. (or: Her car is new.)

ex.t: Il loro figlio ha tre anni.

blocks.tip: {{a casa mia}} “at my place” puts the possessive after the noun, with no article: {{Vieni a casa mia?}} “Do you want to come over to my place?”

mistakes.why: One member of the family: no article. (Pet names keep it: {{la mia mamma}}.)

mistakes.right: Il mio libro è sul tavolo.
mistakes.tr: My book is on the table.
mistakes.why: Things, unlike family members, keep the article: {{il mio libro}}.
{{suo}} agrees with the thing owned: {{moglie}} “wife” is feminine, so {{sua}}, even though Marco is a man.

lessons.title: Ask permission and say what you must do
lessons.summary: Ask if you can pay by card or take a photo, ask for help, and say what you have to and want to do.
lessons.topic: {{potere, dovere, volere}} + the infinitive; {{sapere}} for skills ({{so nuotare}})

goal.t: Posso pagare con la carta?
goal.tr: Can I pay by card?

dialog.tr: Excuse me, can I take a photo?

dialog.t: Sì, ma non può usare il flash.
dialog.tr: Yes, but you can't use the flash.

dialog.t: Va bene. E dove devo lasciare lo zaino?

At the cloakroom, near the entrance.

dialog.t: Grazie. Voglio vedere la Primavera di Botticelli: dov'è?
dialog.tr: Thank you. I want to see Botticelli's Primavera: where is it?

dialog.t: Sala dieci. Deve salire al secondo piano.
dialog.tr: Room ten. You need to go up to the second floor.

blocks.means: a verb like can, must or want, which goes with another verb to say what is possible, necessary or wanted.

blocks.p: **Can, must, want.** {{potere}} “can, may”, {{dovere}} “must, have to” and {{volere}} “to want” are followed by a verb in the infinitive, with nothing in between: {{Posso entrare?}} “May I come in?”, {{Devo andare}} “I have to go”, {{Voglio dormire}} “I want to sleep”.

**Asking.** {{Posso…?}} asks permission: “Can I…?” {{Può…?}} (to {{Lei}}) and {{Puoi…?}} (to {{tu}}) ask for help: {{Può ripetere?}} “Could you repeat that?”, {{Puoi chiamare un taxi?}} “Can you call a taxi?” And {{Vuoi…?}} offers: {{Vuoi un caffè?}} “Do you want a coffee?”

**Can, or know how?** For a skill you've learned, Italian uses {{sapere}} “to know”: {{So nuotare}} “I can swim”, {{Sai cucinare?}} “Can you cook?” ({{so, sai, sa, sappiamo, sapete, sanno}}). {{potere}} is about being able, or allowed, right now: {{Oggi non posso nuotare, ho il raffreddore}} “I can't swim today, I have a cold”.

ex.tr: Do you want to come with us?

ex.t: Deve prendere il treno delle otto.
ex.tr: You need to take the eight o'clock train.
The children want an ice cream.

blocks.tip: {{voglio}} is fine with friends and family, but in a store or a restaurant use {{vorrei}}, the polite form of {{volere}} you met ordering coffee.

mistakes.wrong: Posso a pagare con la carta?
mistakes.why: After {{posso}}, {{devo}} and {{voglio}}, the infinitive follows directly: there's no word for “to”.
A skill you've learned uses {{sapere}}: {{so nuotare}}.

practice.tr: May I open the window?
Tomorrow I have to go to the doctor's.

practice.q: “Can you cook?” (Do you know how?) is…
practice.why: A skill: {{sapere}}. {{Puoi cucinare?}} is “Are you able to cook (now)?”, {{Vuoi cucinare?}} “Do you want to cook?”

lessons.title: Describe your morning routine
lessons.summary: Say when you wake up, get up, get dressed and get ready: the Italian “do it to yourself” verbs.
lessons.topic: Reflexive verbs: {{mi sveglio, ti alzi, si veste}}…; {{devo alzarmi}}

goal.t: Mi sveglio alle sette, mi alzo e mi vesto.
goal.tr: I wake up at seven, I get up and I get dressed.

dialog.t: A che ora ti svegli la mattina?
dialog.tr: What time do you wake up in the morning?

dialog.t: Mi sveglio alle sei e mezza, ma mi alzo alle sette!
dialog.tr: I wake up at six thirty, but I get up at seven!

dialog.t: Io invece mi alzo subito, e mi preparo in dieci minuti.
dialog.tr: I get up right away, and I get ready in ten minutes.

dialog.t: Io mi lavo, mi vesto, faccio colazione... e arrivo sempre in ritardo!
dialog.tr: I wash, get dressed, have breakfast… and I'm always late!

blocks.means: a verb whose action goes back to the subject: “I wash myself”. In the dictionary it ends in {{-si}}: {{lavarsi}} “to wash (yourself)”.

blocks.p: **Doing something to yourself.** Many everyday actions in Italian are reflexive: you wake yourself up, you dress yourself. The verb comes with a little pronoun that matches the subject, placed before it:

Many of them aren't reflexive in English: {{svegliarsi}} “to wake up”, {{alzarsi}} “to get up”, {{vestirsi}} “to get dressed”, {{prepararsi}} “to get ready”, {{sedersi}} “to sit down”, {{divertirsi}} “to have fun”, {{ricordarsi}} “to remember”. And you've known one since the first lesson: {{mi chiamo}} “my name is”, from {{chiamarsi}} “to be called”.

**With {{non}}**, it goes before the little pronoun: {{Non mi alzo presto}} “I don't get up early”. **With a modal verb**, the pronoun can join the end of the infinitive, still matching the subject: {{Devo alzarmi presto}} “I have to get up early”, {{Vuoi sederti?}} “Do you want to sit down?”

ex.tr: What time do you get up?

ex.t: Luca si veste in cinque minuti.
ex.tr: Luca gets dressed in five minutes.
We're having a lot of fun!

ex.t: I bambini si lavano i denti.
ex.note: with body parts, Italian says “the”: {{i denti}}

ex.tr: Tomorrow I have to get up at five.

ex.t: Non mi ricordo il suo nome.

blocks.tip: With your own body and clothes, Italian uses “the”, not “my”: {{Mi lavo le mani}} “I wash my hands”, {{Mi metto la giacca}} “I put on my jacket”. The {{mi}} already says whose.

mistakes.why: {{svegliarsi}} needs its pronoun: {{mi sveglio}}. ({{Sveglio}} alone means “I wake someone else up”.)
With your own body, “the” is enough: {{mi}} already says whose.

mistakes.tr: I have to get up early.
mistakes.why: With a modal verb, the pronoun goes on the end of the infinitive ({{alzarmi}}) or before both verbs ({{Mi devo alzare presto}}), never in between.

practice.tr: In the morning I get up at seven.

practice.q: Talking about weekends: choose your replies.

lessons.title: Say what's happening right now
lessons.summary: On the phone or in a message: “I'm driving”, “It's raining”, “We're on our way!”
lessons.topic: {{stare}} + the gerund: {{sto lavorando, sta piovendo}}

goal.t: Scusa, sto guidando. Ti richiamo dopo!
goal.tr: Sorry, I'm driving. I'll call you back later!

dialog.tr: Hello, sweetheart! What are you doing?

dialog.t: Sto cucinando: stasera vengono Luca e Sara a cena.
dialog.tr: I'm cooking: Luca and Sara are coming for dinner tonight.
And what are you making?

dialog.t: Le lasagne. Ma scusa, sta suonando il campanello!
dialog.tr: Lasagna. But sorry, the doorbell is ringing!
OK, talk to you tomorrow!

blocks.p: **Right now, in the middle of it.** The ordinary present ({{cucino}}) already means both “I cook” and “I'm cooking”. To stress that something is happening at this very moment, Italian uses {{stare}} + the gerund: {{sto cucinando}} “I'm cooking (right now)”.

blocks.means: the -ing form of a verb: cooking, doing. In Italian it ends in {{-ando}} or {{-endo}}: {{parlando}}, {{leggendo}}.

blocks.p: **The gerund**: -are verbs take {{-ando}} ({{parlare → parlando}}), -ere and -ire verbs take {{-endo}} ({{leggere → leggendo}}, {{dormire → dormendo}}). It never changes. Three to learn: {{fare → facendo}}, {{bere → bevendo}}, {{dire → dicendo}} (“saying”).
**Only for what's in progress.** English uses “-ing” for plans too; Italian {{stare}} + gerund is just for now. “I'm leaving tomorrow” is {{Parto domani}}, never {{sto partendo domani}}.

ex.tr: I'm working, I'll call you later.
Excuse me, are you waiting for the doctor?

blocks.tip: {{Arrivo!}} or {{Sto arrivando!}} “Coming!” is what Italians call out when someone rings the doorbell.

mistakes.why: The gerund goes with {{stare}}, not {{essere}}.
{{stare}} + gerund is only for what is happening right now. For plans, use the ordinary present.

practice.tr: I can't talk, I'm driving.
Marco is reading the paper.

practice.why: A plan: the ordinary present. {{stare}} + gerund is only for right now.

lessons.title: Say what you did
lessons.summary: Tell someone what you did yesterday or this morning: “I worked late and ordered a pizza.”
lessons.topic: The passato prossimo with {{avere}}: {{ho lavorato, ho avuto, ho finito}}

goal.t: Ieri ho lavorato tutto il giorno e ho cenato con Sara.
goal.tr: Yesterday I worked all day and had dinner with Sara.

dialog.tr: Hi! Did you finish the project?

dialog.t: Sì, ho finito ieri sera. Ho lavorato fino alle undici!
dialog.tr: Yes, I finished last night. I worked until eleven!
And did you eat?

dialog.t: Sì, ho ordinato una pizza e ho guardato un film.
dialog.tr: Yes, I ordered a pizza and watched a movie.
Did you sleep?

dialog.t: Pochissimo! Stamattina ho bevuto tre caffè.
dialog.tr: Hardly at all! I've had three coffees this morning.

blocks.means: the form of a verb that shows when something happens: present (I live), past (I lived), future (I'll live).

blocks.p: **The past of what happened.** For something you did, Italian uses the {{passato prossimo}}: {{ho}} (from {{avere}}) + the past form of the verb: {{ho lavorato}} “I worked”, {{ho finito}} “I finished”. It covers both the English “I worked” and “I have worked”.

blocks.means: the form of a verb used to make the past: worked, eaten, finished. In Italian: {{lavorato}}, {{avuto}}, {{finito}}.

table: {{Ho avuto un problema.}} “I had a problem.”

blocks.p: Only {{avere}} changes; the participle stays the same for everyone. {{non}} goes before {{ho}}: {{Non ho capito}} “I didn't understand”. A question is the same sentence with the voice going up: {{Hai mangiato?}} “Did you eat? Have you eaten?”
**Time words**: {{ieri}} “yesterday”, {{ieri sera}} “last night”, {{stamattina}} “this morning”, {{oggi}} “today”, {{stasera}} “this evening”.

ex.t: Ieri sera hanno guardato la partita.
ex.tr: Last night they watched the game.

blocks.tip: When you've just missed what someone said, {{Non ho capito}} “I didn't get that” is more natural than {{Non capisco}}.

mistakes.why: The past needs its helper: {{ho}} + {{lavorato}}.
After {{ho}}, the past participle ({{mangiato}}), not the infinitive.
With {{avere}}, the participle doesn't change: {{-ato}} for everyone.

lessons.title: Tell someone about your weekend
lessons.summary: Say what you did, saw, read and took, in order: “First I did the shopping, then I saw a movie.”
lessons.topic: Irregular past participles: {{fatto, visto, preso, detto, letto, scritto, messo}}…; {{prima, poi, alla fine}}

goal.t: Sabato ho fatto una passeggiata e ho visto un bel film.
goal.tr: On Saturday I went for a walk and saw a good movie.

dialog.tr: What did you do over the weekend?

dialog.t: Sabato ho fatto la spesa e ho letto tutto il pomeriggio.
dialog.tr: On Saturday I did the grocery shopping and read all afternoon.
What book did you read?

dialog.t: Un giallo. E domenica ho preso il treno per Verona e ho visto l'Arena!

How lovely! Did you take pictures?
Yes, loads!

blocks.p: **The most common verbs have irregular participles.** You'll use these every day, so learn them as words of their own:
A dictionary gives each verb's participle; these twelve cover most conversations.

**Telling it in order**: {{prima}} “first”, {{poi}} “then”, {{dopo}} “afterwards”, {{alla fine}} “in the end”. {{Prima ho fatto colazione, poi ho preso l'autobus.}} “First I had breakfast, then I took the bus.”

ex.t: Ho fatto una passeggiata al parco.
ex.tr: I went for a walk in the park.

ex.t: Hanno scritto una cartolina alla nonna.
ex.tr: They wrote a postcard to their grandma.

ex.t: Prima ho letto il giornale, poi ho chiamato Marco.
ex.tr: First I read the paper, then I called Marco.

mistakes.why: {{prendere}} has an irregular participle: {{preso}}.
{{vedere}} has an irregular participle: {{visto}}.

lessons.title: Say where you went
lessons.summary: Tell someone where you went, when you left and came back, and whether you liked it: “I went to Naples.”
lessons.topic: The passato prossimo with {{essere}}: {{sono andato / andata}}; {{mi sono svegliato}}; {{mi è piaciuto}}

goal.t: Sono andata a Napoli e sono tornata ieri.
goal.tr: I went to Naples and came back yesterday.
goal.note: said by a woman; a man says {{sono andato… sono tornato}}

dialog.tr: Hi, Giulia! Where have you been?

dialog.t: Sono andata in Sicilia con mia sorella.
dialog.tr: I went to Sicily with my sister.
How lovely! When did you leave?

dialog.t: Siamo partite lunedì e siamo tornate domenica.
dialog.tr: We left on Monday and came back on Sunday.
And did you like it?
Very much! We had a great time.

blocks.p: **Some verbs use {{essere}}, not {{avere}}.** Verbs of going and coming, of staying, and of changing make their past with {{essere}}: {{sono andato}} “I went”, {{sono arrivato}} “I arrived”, {{sono stato}} “I was, I've been”.
**With {{essere}}, the participle agrees** with the subject, like an adjective: a man says {{sono andato}}, a woman {{sono andata}}; a group says {{siamo andati}}, a group of women {{siamo andate}}.

**Reflexive verbs use {{essere}} too**: {{mi sono svegliato}} “I woke up”, {{ci siamo divertiti}} “we had fun”. And so does {{piacere}}, agreeing with the thing you liked: {{Mi è piaciuto il film}} “I liked the movie”, {{Mi è piaciuta la città}} “I liked the city”.

blocks.tip: A quick test: if the verb can take an object (you eat something, you see something), it uses {{avere}}; if it's about moving or changing yourself, it usually uses {{essere}}.

mistakes.why: {{andare}} makes its past with {{essere}}.
With {{essere}}, the participle agrees: Maria is a woman, so {{andata}}.
Reflexive verbs make their past with {{essere}}.

practice.t: Anna e Sara sono ___ in vacanza.
practice.tr: Anna and Sara went on vacation.

practice.why: {{mangiare}} can take an object: {{avere}}. {{uscire}} is about moving: {{essere}}.

lessons.title: Say when it happened, and if it's done yet
lessons.summary: Two days ago, last week, already, just, not yet: put your past in time.
lessons.topic: {{fa}} “ago”, {{scorso}} “last”; {{già}}, {{appena}}, {{non… ancora}}

goal.t: Sono arrivato due giorni fa e ho già visto il Colosseo.
goal.tr: I arrived two days ago and I've already seen the Colosseum.

dialog.tr: When did you arrive in Rome?
Three days ago.

dialog.t: Hai già visto i Musei Vaticani?
dialog.tr: Have you seen the Vatican Museums yet?

dialog.t: Non ancora. Ma ho appena comprato i biglietti per domani!
dialog.tr: Not yet. But I've just bought the tickets for tomorrow!
And the Trevi Fountain?
Yes, last night. Gorgeous!

blocks.p: **When?** {{fa}} after a length of time means “ago”: {{due giorni fa}} “two days ago”, {{un anno fa}} “a year ago”. {{scorso}} “last” agrees with its noun and usually goes after it: {{la settimana scorsa}}, {{il mese scorso}}, {{l'anno scorso}}, {{sabato scorso}}.

**Done yet?** {{già}} “already” and {{appena}} “just” go between the helper and the participle: {{Ho già mangiato}} “I've already eaten”, {{È appena partito}} “He's just left”. {{non… ancora}} is “not yet”: {{Non ho ancora finito}} “I haven't finished yet”, or simply {{Non ancora!}} “Not yet!”
Italian uses the same past for all of these, where English switches between “I ate” and “I've eaten”: {{Ho mangiato un'ora fa}} “I ate an hour ago”, {{Ho già mangiato}} “I've already eaten”.

ex.t: Ho conosciuto Marco un anno fa.
ex.tr: I met Marco a year ago.

ex.t: Il mese scorso siamo andati a Parigi.
ex.tr: Last month we went to Paris.

ex.note: in a question, {{già}} can be “yet” or “already”

blocks.tip: “Ever” in a question is {{mai}}: {{Sei mai stato a Napoli?}} “Have you ever been to Naples?” {{No, mai!}} “No, never!”

mistakes.why: {{fa}} goes after the length of time, just like “ago”.

mistakes.wrong: Il mese scorsa siamo andati a Parigi.
mistakes.right: Il mese scorso siamo andati a Parigi.
mistakes.tr: Last month we went to Paris.
mistakes.why: {{scorso}} agrees with its noun: {{il mese scorso}}, but {{la settimana scorsa}}.

practice.tr: I got home an hour ago.
Last year I changed jobs.
Have you finished already? Yes, I've finished.

practice.q: You're Emma, on vacation in Rome: choose your replies.

lines.t: Hai già visto i Musei Vaticani?
lines.tr: Have you seen the Vatican Museums yet?
When did you arrive?

practice.tr: The train has just left!

practice.q: Your turn: say one thing you did a long time ago, one you did last week, and one you haven't done yet.

answers.t: Dieci anni fa sono andato in Giappone. La settimana scorsa ho visto un concerto. Non ho ancora visto Venezia.
answers.tr: Ten years ago I went to Japan. Last week I saw a concert. I haven't seen Venice yet.

answers.t: Ho imparato a guidare vent'anni fa. Sabato scorso ho fatto una festa. Non ho ancora finito il libro.
answers.tr: I learned to drive twenty years ago. Last Saturday I had a party. I haven't finished the book yet.

lessons.title: Say how long you've been doing something
lessons.summary: “I've been studying Italian for six months”: in Italian, that's the present tense.
lessons.topic: {{da}} + the present ({{abito qui da tre anni}}); {{da quanto tempo…?}}; {{per}} + the past for what is over

goal.t: Studio italiano da sei mesi.
goal.tr: I've been studying Italian for six months.

dialog.t: Da quanto tempo abiti a Bologna?
dialog.tr: How long have you been living in Bologna?
I've been living here for two years.
And since when have you been studying Italian?

dialog.t: Da gennaio. Prima ho studiato spagnolo per cinque anni.
dialog.tr: Since January. Before that I studied Spanish for five years.
Well done, you already speak well!

blocks.p: **Still going on: the present + {{da}}.** For something that started in the past and is still true now, Italian uses the present tense with {{da}}: {{Abito qui da due anni}}, word for word “I live here since two years”. English says “I've been living” or “I've lived” here; Italian doesn't.

table: I've lived here for two years.
We've been waiting for an hour!
How long have you been working here?

blocks.p: {{da}} works for both “for”, a length of time ({{da tre mesi}}), and “since”, a starting point ({{da lunedì}}, {{da gennaio}}, {{dal 2020}}: years take “the”).
**Over and done: the past + {{per}}.** When it's finished, use the passato prossimo with {{per}}: {{Ho abitato a Roma per due anni}} “I lived in Rome for two years” (and I don't anymore).

ex.t: Lavoro in questa azienda da dieci anni.
ex.tr: I've been working at this company for ten years.

ex.t: Non vedo Luca da molto tempo.
ex.tr: I haven't seen Luca for a long time.
ex.note: negative too: it's still true now

ex.tr: We've been married for twenty years.
It's been raining since this morning.
How long have you been waiting?

ex.t: Ho studiato francese per tre anni, a scuola.
ex.tr: I studied French for three years, at school.

blocks.tip: Don't translate “have been”: {{Sono qui da una settimana}} “I've been here for a week” keeps the present of {{essere}}.

mistakes.wrong: Ho abitato qui per due anni.
mistakes.tr: I've been living here for two years.
mistakes.why: If you still live here, use the present with {{da}}. ({{Ho abitato qui per due anni}} means you don't live here anymore.)

mistakes.tr: I've been studying Italian for six months.
mistakes.why: Still going on: {{da}}, not {{per}}.

practice.tr: I've been living in Milan for three years.
How long have you been studying Italian?
practice.why: {{Da quanto tempo…?}} asks how long something has been going on.

practice.q: “I lived in London for five years” (you don't live there anymore) is…
options: {{Ho abitato a Londra per cinque anni.}}
practice.why: It's over: passato prossimo + {{per}}. The other one means you still live there.

practice.q: At a party: choose your replies.

lines.t: Da quanto tempo sei in Italia?
lines.tr: How long have you been in Italy?

options: Sono stato qui per un mese.

lines.tr: And do you like it?

options: Sì, moltissimo! Ma non vedo la mia famiglia da settimane.
Sì, moltissimo! Ma non vedo la mia famiglia per settimane.
lines.why: It's still true now (you still haven't seen them): {{da}}.

practice.tr: We've been waiting for the bus for twenty minutes!

practice.q: Ask your doctor politely: “How long have you been working here?”
Your turn: say how long you've been doing three things: living where you live, your work or studies, learning Italian.

answers.t: Abito a Seattle da otto anni, lavoro in un ospedale da cinque anni e studio italiano da marzo.
answers.tr: I've lived in Seattle for eight years, I've worked in a hospital for five years, and I've been studying Italian since March.

answers.t: Sono sposata da dieci anni e suono la chitarra da quando ho quindici anni.
answers.tr: I've been married for ten years, and I've played the guitar since I was fifteen.

lessons.title: Describe how things used to be
lessons.summary: Talk about your childhood, the old days, what people were like and what you used to do.
lessons.topic: The imperfetto: {{abitavo, avevo, ero, facevo}}; {{c'era, c'erano}}

goal.t: Da bambino abitavo in campagna e andavo a scuola in bicicletta.
goal.tr: As a child I lived in the countryside and rode my bike to school.
goal.note: said by a man; a woman says {{da bambina}}

dialog.t: Nonna, com'era la vita quando eri giovane?
dialog.tr: Grandma, what was life like when you were young?

dialog.t: Era molto diversa! Non avevamo la televisione.
dialog.tr: It was very different! We didn't have a TV.
And what did you do in the evenings?

dialog.t: Parlavamo, giocavamo a carte... e la domenica andavamo a ballare!
dialog.tr: We talked, we played cards… and on Sundays we went dancing!
And did Grandpa dance well?
Terribly! But he was very charming.

blocks.p: **The imperfetto describes the past.** Italian has a second past, the {{imperfetto}}, for what things were like and what used to happen: the background, not the events. {{Abitavo in campagna}} “I lived (used to live) in the countryside”; {{Era una bella giornata}} “It was a beautiful day”.

It's the most regular tense in Italian: take off the {{-re}} of the infinitive and add {{-vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vano}}. Only {{essere}} is really different: {{ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano}}. And three verbs use their old stems: {{fare → facevo}}, {{bere → bevevo}}, {{dire → dicevo}}.

**Use it for** habits in the past ({{Ogni estate andavamo al mare}} “Every summer we went to the beach”); descriptions of people, places, weather and feelings ({{Era stanco}} “He was tired”, {{Faceva freddo}} “It was cold”); age and the time ({{Avevo dieci anni}}, {{Erano le otto}}); and {{c'era, c'erano}} “there was, there were”.

ex.t: Quando ero piccola, avevo un cane.
ex.tr: When I was little, I had a dog.

ex.note: {{fare}} + “the” + a job: what someone did for a living

ex.tr: On Saturdays we used to play soccer.
There were a lot of people in the square.

ex.t: Faceva caldo e il mare era calmo.
ex.tr: It was hot, and the sea was calm.

ex.t: Prima non mi piaceva il caffè.
ex.tr: I didn't use to like coffee.

blocks.tip: {{prima}} “before, I used to” and {{da bambino}} “as a child” are the imperfetto's best friends: {{Prima fumavo, adesso no}} “I used to smoke, now I don't”.

mistakes.wrong: Da bambino ho abitato in campagna e ogni giorno sono andato a scuola a piedi.
mistakes.right: Da bambino abitavo in campagna e ogni giorno andavo a scuola a piedi.
mistakes.tr: As a child I lived in the countryside and walked to school every day.
mistakes.why: Habits and descriptions of the past take the imperfetto.

mistakes.wrong: Quando ho avuto dieci anni, abitavo a Roma.
mistakes.right: Quando avevo dieci anni, abitavo a Roma.
mistakes.tr: When I was ten, I lived in Rome.
mistakes.why: Age in the past is a description: imperfetto.

practice.tr: As a child I always ate pasta.
practice.why: A habit in the past: imperfetto.

practice.tr: When I was twenty, I lived in London.
practice.why: Age uses {{avere}}, and age in the past takes the imperfetto: {{avevo}}.

options: There were a lot of tourists.
There are a lot of tourists.
There have been a lot of tourists.

practice.q: Grandpa tells you about the old days: choose your replies.

lines.t: Quando ero giovane, non c'erano i telefonini!
lines.tr: When I was young, there were no cell phones!

options: E come parlavate con gli amici?
E come avete parlato con gli amici?
lines.why: You're asking about a habit: imperfetto.

lines.t: Andavamo a casa loro, o scrivevamo lettere.
lines.tr: We went to their houses, or we wrote letters.

options: Che bello! E la nonna dove abitava?
Che bello! E la nonna dove abitavo?

practice.tr: Every summer we went to the mountains.

practice.q: Say: “I used to smoke; now I don't anymore.”
practice.answer: Prima fumavo, adesso non fumo più.

practice.q: Your turn: describe your childhood: where did you live, what was your house like, what did you do on weekends?

answers.t: Da bambino abitavo a Chicago. La nostra casa era piccola e il sabato giocavo a baseball con mio padre.
answers.tr: As a child I lived in Chicago. Our house was small, and on Saturdays I played baseball with my father.

answers.t: Quando ero piccola, abitavo al mare. D'estate nuotavamo tutti i giorni.
answers.tr: When I was little, I lived by the sea. In summer we swam every day.

lessons.title: Tell a story
lessons.summary: Set the scene, then say what happened: “While I was waiting for the bus, I ran into Paolo.”
lessons.topic: The imperfetto (the background) and the passato prossimo (the events) together; {{mentre}}

goal.t: Mentre aspettavo l'autobus, ho incontrato Paolo.
goal.tr: While I was waiting for the bus, I ran into Paolo.

dialog.tr: So, how did the trip go?

dialog.t: Un disastro! Era sera e pioveva. Quando siamo arrivati alla stazione, il treno è partito davanti a noi!
dialog.tr: A disaster! It was evening and it was raining. When we got to the station, the train left right in front of us!

dialog.t: Oh no! E cosa avete fatto?
dialog.tr: Oh no! And what did you do?

dialog.t: Eravamo stanchi e avevamo fame, così siamo andati in un bar. E lì abbiamo conosciuto una coppia molto simpatica...
dialog.tr: We were tired and hungry, so we went to a café. And there we met a really nice couple…
And…?

dialog.t: Ci hanno dato un passaggio fino a Firenze!
dialog.tr: They gave us a ride all the way to Florence!

blocks.p: **Two pasts in one story.** A story has a background (what things were like, what was going on) and events (what happened next). Italian gives each its own tense:

table: What was it like? What was going on?
{{Era tardi e pioveva.}} “It was late and it was raining.”

blocks.p: **An action interrupted**: the longer action takes the imperfetto, the one that cuts in takes the passato prossimo: {{Mentre cucinavo, è arrivato Marco}} “While I was cooking, Marco arrived”. Two things going on at the same time both take the imperfetto: {{Mentre io cucinavo, lui leggeva}}.
**The same verb, two meanings.** {{Conoscevo Paolo}} “I knew Paolo (already)”; {{Ho conosciuto Paolo}} “I met Paolo”. {{Sapevo}} “I knew”; {{Ho saputo}} “I found out”.

ex.t: Era una bella giornata, così siamo andati al lago.
ex.tr: It was a beautiful day, so we went to the lake.

ex.t: Mentre dormivo, è suonato il telefono.
ex.tr: While I was sleeping, the phone rang.

ex.t: Non sono uscito perché ero stanco.
ex.tr: I didn't go out because I was tired.
When I came in, everyone was laughing.

ex.t: Avevo fame, quindi ho ordinato una pizza.
ex.tr: I was hungry, so I ordered a pizza.

ex.t: Ieri ho saputo che Anna aspetta un bambino.
ex.tr: Yesterday I found out that Anna is expecting a baby.

blocks.tip: Ask yourself: is it the scenery or the plot? The scenery (weather, time, feelings, what was going on): imperfetto. The plot (one event, then the next): passato prossimo.

mistakes.wrong: Mentre ho cucinato, è arrivato Marco.
mistakes.tr: While I was cooking, Marco arrived.
mistakes.why: The action in progress, the background, takes the imperfetto.

mistakes.wrong: Ho avuto fame, quindi ho ordinato una pizza.
mistakes.right: Avevo fame, quindi ho ordinato una pizza.
mistakes.tr: I was hungry, so I ordered a pizza.
mistakes.why: How you felt is the background: imperfetto. Ordering was the event: passato prossimo.

practice.t: Mentre ___ la TV, è andata via la luce.
practice.tr: While I was watching TV, the power went out.
It was late, so we took a taxi.
practice.why: The event: passato prossimo, with the irregular {{preso}}.

practice.q: {{Ho conosciuto Paolo a una festa}} means…
options: I met Paolo at a party.
I knew Paolo from a party.
I used to know Paolo at parties.
practice.why: {{conoscere}} in the passato prossimo means meeting someone for the first time.

practice.q: A friend asks about last night: choose your replies.

lines.t: Perché non sei venuto alla festa?
lines.tr: Why didn't you come to the party?
Too bad! So what did you do?

options: Sono rimasto a casa e ho dormito.
lines.why: The events of the evening: passato prossimo.

practice.tr: While I was walking, I saw an old friend.

practice.q: Say (as a woman): “It was raining, so I stayed home.”
practice.answer: Pioveva, quindi sono rimasta a casa.

practice.q: Your turn: tell a short story about something unexpected. Set the scene (where you were, the weather, what you were doing), then say what happened.

answers.t: Ero in un bar a Roma e bevevo un caffè. All'improvviso è entrato un attore famoso!
answers.tr: I was in a café in Rome, having a coffee. Suddenly a famous actor walked in!

answers.t: Era domenica e faceva bel tempo. Mentre camminavo nel parco, ho trovato un portafoglio con cento euro.
answers.tr: It was Sunday and the weather was nice. While I was walking in the park, I found a wallet with a hundred euros in it.

lessons.title: Avoid repeating yourself when you shop
lessons.summary: “I'll take it”, “Can I try them on?”, “I can't find them!”: replace the thing with a short word.
lessons.topic: Direct object pronouns {{lo, la, li, le}} (and {{mi, ti, ci, vi}}) before the verb; {{l'ho comprata}}

goal.t: Questa giacca mi piace molto: la prendo!
goal.tr: I really like this jacket: I'll take it!

dialog.tr: Do you like these shoes?
Yes, a lot. Can I try them on?
Of course. What size do you wear?

dialog.t: Il trentanove... Mi stanno bene! Le prendo.
dialog.tr: A thirty-nine… They fit! I'll take them.
Perfect. And the bag?

dialog.t: La borsa no, grazie: non la uso mai.
dialog.tr: Not the bag, thanks: I never use one.

blocks.p: **Not saying the noun twice.** Once you've named something, replace it with a short pronoun that goes **before** the verb: {{Prendo la giacca}} → {{La prendo}} “I'll take it”.

blocks.means: the person or thing that receives the action of the verb, with no preposition before it: in “I see Marco”, Marco is the direct object.

table: me, you, us, you (two or more)

blocks.p: **It agrees.** “It” is {{lo}} for a masculine thing and {{la}} for a feminine one: the pronoun takes the gender of the noun it replaces. Before a vowel or an h, {{lo}} and {{la}} become {{l'}}: {{L'ho visto}} “I saw it, I saw him”.
**Where it goes**: before the verb, and after {{non}}: {{Non lo compro}} “I'm not buying it”. With an infinitive, it can join the end: {{Posso provarla?}} or {{La posso provare?}} “Can I try it on?”
**In the past**, after {{l'}}, {{li}} and {{le}}, the participle agrees with the pronoun: {{La giacca? L'ho comprata ieri.}} {{Le scarpe? Le ho prese.}}

ex.t: Il caffè lo prendi con lo zucchero?
ex.tr: Do you take your coffee with sugar?
ex.note: Italians often name the thing first, then use the pronoun

ex.t: Conosci Marco? Sì, lo conosco bene.
ex.tr: Do you know Marco? Yes, I know him well.

ex.t: Dove sono le chiavi? Non le trovo!
ex.tr: Where are the keys? I can't find them!
I'll wait for you in front of the movie theater.

ex.t: Hai visto il film? Sì, l'ho visto ieri.
ex.tr: Have you seen the movie? Yes, I saw it yesterday.

blocks.tip: {{questo}} “this” and {{quello}} “that” agree like adjectives: {{questo libro}}, {{questa giacca}}, {{questi pantaloni}}, {{queste scarpe}}. In a store, point and say {{questo qui}} “this one here”.

mistakes.why: The pronoun goes before the verb.
{{scarpe}} is feminine plural: {{le}}.

mistakes.tr: The jacket? I bought it yesterday.
mistakes.why: After a pronoun for a feminine thing, the participle agrees: {{comprata}}.

practice.tr: The newspaper? I'll buy it.
The keys? I can't find them!

practice.why: {{ti}} “you” is the object; the verb {{chiamo}} says “I”. And the present works for plans.

practice.q: In a clothing store: choose your replies.

lines.tr: Do you like this sweater?
Of course! The fitting room is over there.

lines.why: The pronoun goes before the verb: {{lo prendo}}.

practice.tr: I saw them yesterday at the station.

practice.q: A friend asks if you've read the book ({{il libro}}). Answer: “Yes, I read it last month.”
practice.answer: Sì, l'ho letto il mese scorso.

practice.q: Your turn: you're shopping. Say what you'll take and what you won't, without repeating the nouns: {{la prendo}}, {{non lo prendo}}…

answers.t: La giacca la prendo, ma le scarpe no: sono troppo care.
answers.tr: I'll take the jacket, but not the shoes: they're too expensive.

answers.t: Questi jeans mi piacciono: li prendo!
answers.tr: I like these jeans: I'll take them!

lessons.title: Say who you give, tell or write things to
lessons.summary: Presents, messages and phone calls: “I'm giving her a book”, “I'll call him tonight”.
lessons.topic: Indirect object pronouns {{mi, ti, gli, le, Le, ci, vi}}; {{gli piace}}

goal.t: Domani è il compleanno di Anna: le compro dei fiori.
goal.tr: Tomorrow is Anna's birthday: I'm buying her some flowers.

dialog.t: Cosa regali a tua madre per Natale?
dialog.tr: What are you giving your mother for Christmas?

dialog.t: Le regalo un libro di cucina. E tu, cosa regali a tuo padre?
dialog.tr: I'm giving her a cookbook. And you, what are you giving your father?

dialog.t: Gli regalo una cravatta, come sempre!
dialog.tr: I'm giving him a tie, as always!
And your grandparents?

dialog.t: Gli mando un cesto di prodotti tipici.
dialog.tr: I'm sending them a basket of local specialties.

dialog.t: Che bella idea! Mi dai l'indirizzo del negozio?
dialog.tr: What a nice idea! Can you give me the store's address?

blocks.p: **To whom?** Many verbs have a person who receives something: you give to someone, tell, write, send, phone, ask. That person becomes a short pronoun before the verb:

blocks.means: the person who receives or benefits from the action, usually after “to” or “for” in English: in “I give a book to Anna”, Anna is the indirect object.

table: {{Mi dai il sale?}} “Can you pass me the salt?”
{{Ti scrivo domani.}} “I'll write to you tomorrow.”
{{Le regalo un libro.}} “I'm giving her a book.”
{{Le porto il menù.}} “I'll bring you the menu.”
{{Ci mandi le foto?}} “Will you send us the photos?”
{{Vi preparo un caffè.}} “I'll make you a coffee.”
{{Gli spiego la strada.}} “I'll explain the way to them.”

blocks.p: **Not the same as the last lesson.** {{lo}} and {{la}} are the person or thing you see, take or call; {{gli}} and {{le}} are the person you give to, tell, or write to. Watch two verbs: {{telefonare a}} “to phone” takes {{gli, le}}: {{Le telefono}} “I'll call her”; {{chiamare}} takes {{lo, la}}: {{La chiamo}} “I'll call her”.
**You've used them already**: {{mi piace}} is “it is pleasing to me”, so {{gli piace}} is “he likes”, {{le piace}} “she likes”, and {{Le piace}} “you like”, to {{Lei}}.

ex.tr: Can you lend me your pen?

ex.note: {{far vedere}} “to show”, word for word “to make see”

ex.t: A Marco piace il pesce? No, non gli piace.
ex.tr: Does Marco like fish? No, he doesn't.

blocks.tip: {{gli}} for “to them” is normal in everyday Italian. In very formal writing you may see {{loro}} after the verb instead: {{Do loro un libro}}.

mistakes.why: {{telefonare}} is “to phone to” someone: {{gli}}, not {{lo}}.
“She likes” is {{le piace}}: “it pleases (to) her”. {{lei}} is “she” as the subject.

practice.t: È il compleanno di Sara: ___ compro una torta.
practice.tr: It's Sara's birthday: I'm buying her a cake.

practice.t: Marco non risponde. ___ mando un messaggio.
practice.tr: Marco isn't answering. I'll send him a message.

practice.why: {{gli}} is “to him”: “soccer is pleasing to him”.

lines.tr: What are you giving your brother?
And your sister?
And me?

options: A te? Ti offro un caffè!
A te? Mi offro un caffè!
lines.why: To you: {{ti}}. ({{Mi offro}} would be “I offer myself”!)

practice.tr: I'll call her tonight.

practice.q: Ask the waiter politely: “Could you bring me the check, please?”
practice.answer: Mi può portare il conto, per favore?

practice.q: Your turn: someone you know has a birthday soon. Say what you'll give them, and one more thing you'll do for them (write, call, cook).

answers.t: Mio padre compie sessant'anni: gli regalo un orologio e gli preparo una cena.
answers.tr: My father is turning sixty: I'm giving him a watch and making him dinner.

answers.t: Domani è il compleanno di Giulia: le scrivo un biglietto e le compro dei fiori.
answers.tr: Tomorrow is Giulia's birthday: I'm writing her a card and buying her some flowers.

lessons.title: Buy food at the market
lessons.summary: Ask for some tomatoes, say how much you want, and understand “we don't have any”.
lessons.topic: {{ne}} “of it, of them” with amounts: {{ne vorrei un chilo, non ne ho}}; “some”: {{del, della, dei, delle}}

goal.t: Vorrei delle mele. Ne prendo un chilo.
goal.tr: I'd like some apples. I'll take a kilo.

dialog.tr: Good morning, madam! What can I get you?
I'd like some tomatoes.
How many would you like?

dialog.t: Ne prendo mezzo chilo. E avete fragole?
dialog.tr: I'll take half a kilo. And do you have strawberries?

dialog.t: Mi dispiace, oggi non ne abbiamo.
dialog.tr: Sorry, we don't have any today.

dialog.t: Va bene. Allora vorrei del formaggio: ne vorrei due etti.
dialog.tr: OK. Then I'd like some cheese: two hundred grams, please.

blocks.p: **{{ne}}: of it, of them.** When you say how much or how many of something, Italian doesn't leave the number on its own: it adds {{ne}} “of it, of them” before the verb. {{Quante mele vuole?}} {{Ne vorrei tre}}, word for word “Of them I'd like three”.

table: How old are you? I'm thirty.

blocks.p: **Where it goes**: before the verb, like {{lo}} and {{la}}: {{Ne compro tre}}; with an infinitive, it can join the end: {{Voglio comprarne tre}}. With {{non}}: {{Non ne ho}} “I don't have any”.

**Some**: before a noun, {{di}} + “the” means “some”: {{del pane}}, {{della frutta}}, {{dei pomodori}}, {{delle mele}}. In questions and negatives it's usually left out: {{Avete fragole?}}, {{Non ho tempo}}.

ex.t: Quanti figli hai? Ne ho due.
ex.tr: How many children do you have? I have two.

ex.t: Vuoi un caffè? No, grazie, ne ho già bevuti tre!
ex.tr: Do you want a coffee? No, thanks, I've already had three!
ex.note: in the past, the participle agrees with what {{ne}} counts

ex.t: Mi servono delle uova. Ne compri sei?
ex.tr: I need some eggs. Can you buy six?

ex.t: C'è ancora latte? No, non ce n'è più.
ex.tr: Is there any milk left? No, there's none left.

lessons.title: Talk about going there
lessons.summary: “I go there every summer”, “Have you ever been there?”, “How long does it take?”
lessons.topic: {{ci}} “there”: {{ci vado, ci sono stato}}; {{ci vuole, ci vogliono}} “it takes”

goal.t: Roma? Ci vado ogni anno!
goal.tr: Rome? I go there every year!

dialog.tr: Have you ever been to Sardinia?

dialog.t: No, non ci sono mai stato. E tu?
dialog.tr: No, I've never been there. And you?

dialog.t: Io ci vado ogni estate. Quest'anno ci vado ad agosto con la famiglia.
dialog.tr: I go there every summer. This year I'm going in August with my family.
How do you get there?

dialog.t: In traghetto da Livorno. Ci vogliono dieci ore!
dialog.tr: By ferry from Livorno. It takes ten hours!
Ten hours? What patience!

blocks.p: **{{ci}}: there.** Once a place has been named, {{ci}} replaces it, before the verb: {{Vai a Roma? Sì, ci vado domani}} “Are you going to Rome? Yes, I'm going (there) tomorrow”. Italian says it where English often leaves “there” out.
**You know it already**: {{c'è}} and {{ci sono}} are {{ci}} + {{essere}}: “there is, there are”.
**{{ci vuole, ci vogliono}}** means “it takes”, time or things: {{Ci vuole un'ora}} “It takes an hour”, {{Ci vogliono tre uova}} “It takes three eggs”. The verb agrees with what it takes.
Don't mix it up with {{ci}} “us, each other”: {{Ci vediamo domani}} “See you tomorrow”, word for word “We see each other tomorrow”. The sentence makes it clear.

ex.t: Il mare? Ci andiamo ogni domenica.
ex.tr: The beach? We go there every Sunday.

ex.t: Sei mai stata a Venezia? Sì, ci sono stata due volte.
ex.tr: Have you ever been to Venice? Yes, I've been there twice.

ex.t: Quanto ci vuole per arrivare in centro?
ex.tr: How long does it take to get downtown?

ex.t: Ci vogliono venti minuti a piedi.
ex.tr: It takes twenty minutes on foot.

ex.t: Vado in farmacia. Ci vieni anche tu?
ex.tr: I'm going to the pharmacy. Are you coming too?
I don't think about it anymore.
ex.note: after {{pensare a}}, {{ci}} also stands for “about it”

blocks.tip: {{Ci penso io!}} “I'll take care of it!” is one of the handiest phrases in Italian.

mistakes.why: {{essere}} and {{stare}} make their past with {{essere}}: {{ci sono stato}}.
The verb agrees with what it takes: {{due ore}} is plural, so {{ci vogliono}}.

lessons.title: Compare things
lessons.summary: Choose between two apartments, two trains or two restaurants: bigger, cheaper, better.
lessons.topic: {{più / meno… di}}; {{di}} or {{che}}; {{migliore, peggiore, meglio, peggio}}; {{come}}

goal.t: Il treno è più comodo dell'aereo, ma è meno veloce.
goal.tr: The train is more comfortable than the plane, but it's slower.

dialog.tr: So, which apartment are you taking?

dialog.t: Non so. Quello in centro è più bello, ma è più caro.
dialog.tr: I don't know. The one downtown is nicer, but it's more expensive.
And the other one?

dialog.t: È più grande e meno caro, ma è lontano dal lavoro.
dialog.tr: It's bigger and cheaper, but it's far from work.

dialog.t: Secondo me è meglio vivere in centro. Spendi di più, ma vivi meglio!
dialog.tr: If you ask me, it's better to live downtown. You spend more, but you live better!

blocks.p: **More, less.** {{più}} “more” or {{meno}} “less” goes before the adjective, and {{di}} “than” before what you compare it with. {{di}} joins “the”: {{più alto di Marco}}, {{più caro del treno}}, {{più comodo dell'aereo}}.

**{{di}} or {{che}}?** Use {{di}} before a noun, a name or a pronoun: {{Roma è più grande di Firenze}}, {{è più alto di me}}. Use {{che}} when the two things you compare come after a preposition, or are two adjectives: {{Fa più caldo a Roma che a Milano}} “It's hotter in Rome than in Milan”; {{È più bello che utile}} “It's more beautiful than useful”.

**Better, worse.** {{buono}} has its own forms: {{migliore}} “better” and {{peggiore}} “worse”, used with nouns. With verbs, “better” is {{meglio}} and “worse” {{peggio}}: {{Parli meglio di me}} “You speak better than me”. And {{è meglio}} + infinitive is “it's better to…”.

ex.t: Mio fratello è più alto di me.
ex.tr: My brother is taller than me.

ex.t: Questo vino è migliore di quello.
ex.tr: This wine is better than that one.

ex.t: Il treno è meno caro dell'aereo.
ex.tr: The train is cheaper than the plane.

ex.t: A Roma fa più caldo che a Milano.
ex.tr: It's hotter in Rome than in Milan.

ex.t: Luca è simpatico come suo padre.
ex.tr: Luca is as nice as his father.

blocks.tip: At the end of a sentence, “more” is {{di più}}: {{Lavoro di più}} “I work more”; {{Mi piace di più il mare}} “I like the sea better”.

mistakes.wrong: Roma è più grande che Firenze.
mistakes.right: Roma è più grande di Firenze.
mistakes.why: Before a noun or a name, “than” is {{di}}.
“Better” with a verb is {{meglio}}.
{{migliore}} already means “better”: no {{più}}.
