lessons.title: Say what's the best
lessons.summary: Recommend the best pizzeria, the most beautiful beach, and say something is amazing: {{buonissimo!}}
lessons.topic: The superlative: {{il più… di}}; {{il migliore}}; {{-issimo}}

goal.t: È la pizzeria migliore della città!
goal.tr: It's the best pizzeria in town!

dialog.t: Qual è il museo più interessante di Firenze?
dialog.tr: What's the most interesting museum in Florence?

dialog.t: Gli Uffizi, senza dubbio. Ma sono anche i più affollati!
dialog.tr: The Uffizi, without a doubt. But it's also the most crowded!
And the best gelato?

dialog.t: In una gelateria piccolissima vicino a Santa Croce. È buonissimo!
dialog.tr: In a tiny gelato shop near Santa Croce. It's amazing!

dialog.t: Perfetto, è la cosa più importante!
dialog.tr: Perfect, that's the most important thing!

blocks.p: **The most…** Italian makes “the most” with “the” + {{più}}: {{il più caro}} “the most expensive”, {{la più bella}} “the most beautiful”. With a noun, the noun usually goes in between: {{il ristorante più caro}} “the most expensive restaurant”. “In” the city, the world or the group is {{di}}: {{il più alto della classe}} “the tallest in the class”.

table: the best pizza in the world

blocks.p: **Very, very: {{-issimo}}.** To say something is extremely good, beautiful or expensive, without comparing it, drop the adjective's last vowel and add {{-issimo}}: {{buono → buonissimo}}, {{bella → bellissima}}, {{cari → carissimi}}. It agrees like any adjective, and Italians use it all the time: {{Grazie, sei gentilissima!}}
The same works for {{bene → benissimo}} “very well”, {{molto → moltissimo}} “very much”, {{tanto → tantissimo}}.

ex.t: È la città più bella del mondo.
ex.tr: It's the most beautiful city in the world.

ex.t: Qual è il piatto più tipico della zona?
ex.tr: What's the most typical dish around here?

ex.t: Questo è il periodo migliore per visitare la Sicilia.
ex.tr: This is the best time to visit Sicily.

ex.note: {{lungo → lunghissimo}}: an h keeps the g hard

ex.t: Mio padre è il più giovane dei suoi fratelli.
ex.tr: My father is the youngest of his brothers.

blocks.tip: {{il migliore}} can stand alone, as in English: {{Sei il migliore!}} “You're the best!” (to a woman: {{Sei la migliore!}}).

mistakes.wrong: È il più grande ristorante in Roma.
mistakes.right: È il ristorante più grande di Roma.
mistakes.tr: It's the biggest restaurant in Rome.
mistakes.why: The noun first, then {{più}} + adjective; and “in” the city is {{di}}.
{{-issimo}} already means “very”: no {{molto}}.

practice.t: Marco è il più alto ___ classe.
practice.tr: Marco is the tallest in the class.

lessons.title: Talk about the future
lessons.summary: Say what you'll do next year, make promises and predictions, and make a guess: “He's probably at home.”
lessons.topic: The futuro semplice: {{parlerò, prenderò, sarò, andrò}}; the future for guesses

goal.t: L'anno prossimo andrò in Italia e studierò a Firenze.
goal.tr: Next year I'll go to Italy and study in Florence.

dialog.tr: What will you do after college?

dialog.t: Lavorerò un anno, poi viaggerò in Sud America.
dialog.tr: I'll work for a year, then I'll travel around South America.
How lovely! And where will you live?
I don't know yet. We'll see!
It'll be an adventure!

blocks.p: **The future is one word in Italian.** Take off the final {{-e}} of the infinitive and add {{-ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno}}; -are verbs also change their {{a}} to {{e}}: {{parlare → parlerò}}.

**Irregular, but in a pattern.** Several common verbs shorten their stem; the endings stay the same: {{essere → sarò}}, {{avere → avrò}}, {{andare → andrò}}, {{fare → farò}}, {{potere → potrò}}, {{dovere → dovrò}}, {{vedere → vedrò}}, {{sapere → saprò}}, {{venire → verrò}}, {{volere → vorrò}}, {{bere → berrò}}, {{rimanere → rimarrò}}.

**When do Italians use it?** For plans already fixed, the present is enough ({{Domani parto}}). The future is for what's further away or less certain, for promises and for predictions: {{Ti chiamerò}} “I'll call you”, {{Domani pioverà}} “It will rain tomorrow”. “In” a length of time from now is {{tra}} or {{fra}}: {{tra cinque anni}} “in five years”.
**Guessing.** The future also says what is probably true right now: {{Dov'è Marco? Sarà a casa}} “Where's Marco? He's probably at home”; {{Che ore sono? Saranno le dieci}} “It must be about ten”.

ex.t: Un giorno avrò una casa al mare.
ex.tr: One day I'll have a house by the sea.
When will you finish the book?
Will you come to the party?

ex.t: Tra due settimane saremo in vacanza.
ex.tr: In two weeks we'll be on vacation.

ex.t: Chi è alla porta? Sarà il postino.
ex.tr: Who's at the door? It's probably the mailman.

blocks.tip: Verbs in {{-care}} and {{-gare}} add an h to keep the hard sound: {{cercare → cercherò}}, {{pagare → pagherò}}. Verbs in {{-ciare}} and {{-giare}} drop their i: {{cominciare → comincerò}}, {{mangiare → mangerò}}.

mistakes.why: -are verbs change their a to e in the future: {{parlerò}}.

mistakes.tr: Next year I'll go to Sicily.
mistakes.why: {{andare}} shortens its stem: {{andrò}}.

practice.tr: Next summer we'll go to Greece.
practice.why: {{andare}} → {{andr-}}, and {{-emo}} is “we”. ({{andremmo}}, with two m's, means “we would go”.)

practice.tr: The weather will be nice tomorrow.

options: Where's Luca? He's probably at the office.
Where's Luca? He was at the office.
Where's Luca? He has to be at the office.
practice.why: The future can be a guess about now: “he's probably…”.

Lavorarò un anno e poi viaggiarò.

lessons.title: Say what will happen if…
lessons.summary: Make plans that depend on something: “If it rains, we'll stay home”, “As soon as I arrive, I'll call you.”
lessons.topic: {{se}} + the present (or the future); {{quando}}, {{appena}}

goal.t: Se domani piove, restiamo a casa.
goal.tr: If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay home.

dialog.tr: Shall we have a picnic on Sunday?

dialog.t: Sì! Se fa bel tempo, andiamo al lago.
dialog.tr: Yes! If the weather's nice, let's go to the lake.
And if it rains?

dialog.t: Se piove, veniamo da te e guardiamo un film.
dialog.tr: If it rains, we'll come to your place and watch a movie.

dialog.t: Perfetto. Se vuoi, preparo io i panini.
dialog.tr: Perfect. If you like, I'll make the sandwiches.

dialog.t: Se li prepari tu, io porto il dolce!
dialog.tr: If you make them, I'll bring dessert!

blocks.p: **Real possibilities.** {{se}} “if” + the present, then the result, also in the present (or the future): {{Se piove, restiamo a casa}}. In everyday speech, the present in both halves is the most common.

table: {{andiamo al cinema.}} “let's go to the movies.”

blocks.p: **Further ahead**: when both halves are clearly in the future, careful Italian puts both in the future: {{Se avrò tempo, verrò}} “If I have time, I'll come”. English never uses “will” after “if”; Italian can.

**When, as soon as**: {{quando}} and {{appena}} work the same way: {{Quando arrivo, ti chiamo}} or {{Quando arriverò, ti chiamerò}} “When I arrive, I'll call you”; {{Appena finisco, esco}} “As soon as I finish, I'm going out”. And “unless” is simply {{se non}}: {{Se non piove, andiamo al mare}}.

ex.t: Se hai fame, c'è della pizza in frigo.
ex.tr: If you're hungry, there's some pizza in the fridge.

ex.t: Se vuoi, ti accompagno alla stazione.
ex.tr: If you like, I'll walk you to the station.

ex.t: Se perdi l'autobus, prendi un taxi.
ex.tr: If you miss the bus, take a taxi.

ex.t: Se non ti piace, puoi cambiarlo.
ex.tr: If you don't like it, you can exchange it.

ex.t: Se finiremo presto, andremo al ristorante.
ex.tr: If we finish early, we'll go to a restaurant.

ex.t: Appena arrivo a casa, ti scrivo.
ex.tr: As soon as I get home, I'll text you.

ex.t: Quando sarò in pensione, viaggerò tanto.
ex.tr: When I'm retired, I'll travel a lot.

blocks.tip: {{Se vuoi}} and {{se ti va}} “if you like, if you feel like it” are the friendly way to offer: {{Se ti va, ceniamo insieme}} “If you feel like it, let's have dinner together”.

mistakes.tr: If I have time, I'll come.
mistakes.why: After {{se}}, never a “would” form like {{vorrei}} or {{avrei}}: for a real possibility, use the present.

mistakes.tr: If you like, I'll help you.
mistakes.why: “I'll help you” is {{ti aiuto}}: the pronoun goes before the verb.

practice.tr: If we have time, we'll come and see you.
practice.why: After {{se}}, for a real possibility: the present.

practice.why: “You can” ({{tu}}): {{puoi}}, followed directly by the infinitive.

options: As soon as I arrive, I'll call you.
If I arrive, I'll call you.

practice.why: {{appena}} + a verb in the present is “as soon as”. (With the past, {{sono appena arrivato}}, it means “I've just arrived”.)

lessons.title: Ask politely and give advice
lessons.summary: “Could you…?”, “You should…”, “I'd love to…”: the condizionale, Italian's polite and dreaming form.
lessons.topic: The condizionale: {{potrebbe, dovresti, mi piacerebbe, al tuo posto…}}

goal.t: Potrebbe chiamarmi un taxi, per favore?
goal.tr: Could you call me a taxi, please?

dialog.t: Non dormo bene e sono sempre stanco.
dialog.tr: I don't sleep well and I'm always tired.
You should drink less coffee.

dialog.t: Lo so... E poi lavoro troppo.
dialog.tr: I know… And I work too much.

dialog.t: Al tuo posto, prenderei qualche giorno di ferie.
dialog.tr: If I were you, I'd take a few days off.

dialog.t: Mi piacerebbe tanto! Andrei al mare...
dialog.tr: I'd love to! I'd go to the beach…
So why don't you do it?

blocks.p: **“Would”: the condizionale.** You've used it since the café: {{vorrei}} “I'd like”. It's the polite form of everything, and the way to give advice and talk about wishes. It's built like the future, with {{-ei}} endings instead: {{parlerò}} “I'll speak” → {{parlerei}} “I'd speak”.
The future's short stems come back: {{sarei}}, {{avrei}}, {{andrei}}, {{farei}}, {{dovrei}}, {{verrei}}. Watch the double m: {{parleremo}} “we'll speak”, {{parleremmo}} “we'd speak”.

**Three everyday jobs.** Asking politely: {{Potrebbe aiutarmi?}} “Could you help me?”. Giving advice: {{Dovresti riposarti}} “You should rest”, {{Al tuo posto, andrei dal medico}} “If I were you, I'd go to the doctor”. Wishes: {{Mi piacerebbe vivere in Italia}} “I'd love to live in Italy”, {{Sarebbe bello!}} “That would be nice!”

ex.tr: We'd like a table for four.
I'd love to learn to cook.

ex.t: Al posto tuo, non direi niente.
ex.tr: If I were you, I wouldn't say anything.
It would be better to leave early.

blocks.tip: The condizionale softens anything: {{Avrei una domanda}} “I'd have a question” sounds gentler than {{Ho una domanda}}.

mistakes.tr: I'd love to go to Italy.
mistakes.why: {{piacere}} agrees with what you'd like (here, going): {{piacerebbe}}, just as you say {{mi piace}}.
As with {{devo}}, the infinitive follows directly.
Polite “could we”: {{potremmo}}, with two m's. {{potremo}} means “we will be able to”.

practice.tr: I'd like a coffee, please.

practice.t: Sei stanco: ___ andare a letto presto.

lessons.title: Give instructions to a friend
lessons.summary: Teach a recipe, tell a friend what to do and what not to: “Stir it!”, “Don't worry!”, “Tell me!”
lessons.topic: The imperative for {{tu}} and {{voi}}; {{non}} + infinitive; pronouns on the end: {{prendilo, dimmi}}

goal.t: Metti la pasta nell'acqua e girala ogni tanto!
goal.tr: Put the pasta in the water and stir it now and then!

dialog.t: Allora, prima metti l'acqua sul fuoco.
dialog.tr: So, first put the water on the stove.
And the salt?

dialog.t: Aspetta... Ecco, bolle: aggiungi il sale e butta la pasta.
dialog.tr: Wait… There, it's boiling: add the salt and throw in the pasta.
Shall I stir it?

dialog.t: Sì, girala ogni tanto. E non cuocerla troppo!
dialog.tr: Yes, stir it now and then. And don't overcook it!
How many minutes?

dialog.t: Leggi sulla confezione. Dieci minuti, al dente!
dialog.tr: Read the package. Ten minutes, al dente!

blocks.means: the form of a verb for telling someone what to do: Look! Wait! Come in!

blocks.p: **Telling a friend what to do.** The {{tu}} imperative of -ere and -ire verbs is the same as the present: {{prendi!}} “take!”, {{senti!}} “listen!”. For -are verbs it ends in {{-a}}: {{guarda!}} “look!”, {{aspetta!}} “wait!”. For two or more people ({{voi}}), it's simply the present: {{guardate!}}, {{prendete!}}, {{sentite!}}
**Don't!** For {{tu}}, the negative is {{non}} + the infinitive: {{Non toccare!}} “Don't touch!”, {{Non preoccuparti!}} “Don't worry!”. For {{voi}}, just {{non}} + the imperative: {{Non toccate!}}

**Pronouns join the end**: {{Prendilo!}} “Take it!”, {{Girala!}} “Stir it!”, {{Aspettami!}} “Wait for me!”. After the short forms {{va', fa', di', da'}}, the pronoun's first letter doubles: {{Dimmi!}} “Tell me!”, {{Fammi vedere!}} “Let me see!”, {{Dammi!}} “Give me!”
**Let's…**: the “we” form of the present: {{Andiamo!}} “Let's go!”, {{Mangiamo!}} “Let's eat!”

ex.tr: Don't worry, I'll take care of it.

ex.t: Non fate rumore, il bambino dorme.
ex.tr: Don't make noise, the baby's sleeping.

ex.t: Fammi un favore: chiudi la finestra.
ex.tr: Do me a favor: close the window.

blocks.tip: {{Dai!}} (from {{dare}} “to give”) is everywhere: “Come on!”. And {{Senti…}} or {{Scusa…}} is how you get a friend's attention.

mistakes.why: “Don't” to a friend: {{non}} + the infinitive.

lessons.title: Ask for and give directions politely
lessons.summary: Understand and give directions to a stranger: “Go straight ahead and turn left.” Plus the polite words you hear in every store.
lessons.topic: The imperative for {{Lei}}: {{scusi, vada, giri, prenda, mi dica, si accomodi}}

goal.t: Vada sempre dritto e giri alla seconda a destra.
goal.tr: Keep going straight ahead and take the second right.

dialog.t: Scusi, mi sa dire come arrivare alla stazione?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, can you tell me how to get to the station?

dialog.t: Certo. Attraversi la piazza e prenda via Garibaldi.
dialog.tr: Of course. Cross the square and take Via Garibaldi.
Via Garibaldi… and then?

dialog.t: Vada sempre dritto fino al semaforo, poi giri a destra. La stazione è lì.
dialog.tr: Go straight ahead as far as the traffic light, then turn right. The station is right there.
Is it far?

dialog.t: No, dieci minuti a piedi. Ma faccia attenzione al traffico!
dialog.tr: No, ten minutes on foot. But watch out for the traffic!
Thank you so much, that's very kind!

blocks.p: **Telling someone you call {{Lei}} what to do** uses its own form: the vowels swap. -are verbs end in {{-i}}: {{giri!}} “turn!”, {{scusi!}} “excuse me!”. -ere and -ire verbs end in {{-a}}: {{prenda!}} “take!”, {{senta!}} “listen!”

You hear many of these all day in stores and offices: {{Mi dica!}} “How can I help you?”, word for word “Tell me!”; {{Prego, si accomodi}} “Please, have a seat” or “come in”; {{Senta, scusi…}} “Excuse me…”, to get someone's attention; {{Attenda in linea}} “Please hold”.
**The pronouns stay in front** with {{Lei}}: {{Mi dica}}, {{La prenda}} “Take it”, {{Si accomodi}}. And “don't” is just {{non}} + the same form: {{Non si preoccupi}} “Don't worry”.

**Keep these forms in mind.** {{vada, prenda, faccia, venga, dica}} are also the forms of the {{congiuntivo}}, the subjunctive, which the next unit uses for opinions and wishes. You're already halfway there.

ex.tr: Turn left at the traffic light.

ex.t: Prenda la seconda strada a destra.
ex.tr: Take the second street on the right.

ex.t: Non si preoccupi, non è niente.

blocks.tip: To ask: {{Scusi, sa dov'è…?}} “Excuse me, do you know where … is?” or {{Mi sa dire come arrivare a…?}} “Can you tell me how to get to…?”. The answers often include {{sempre dritto}} “straight ahead”, {{all'incrocio}} “at the intersection” and {{al semaforo}} “at the traffic light”.
